title: Natural Barriers to Quantum Extraction: On the Post-Quantum (In)security of (O)EKE and Masny-Rindal OT
abstract: Encrypted key exchange (EKE), introduced by Bellovin and Merritt (IEEE S\&P 1992), and Masny-Rindal OT, introduced by Masny and Rindal (ACM CCS 2019), are highly-efficient methods for compiling essentially any KEM into advanced cryptographic protocols, namely password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) and oblivious transfer (OT), by relying only on idealized symmetric-key primitives. They have become leading candidates for practically-implementable PAKE and OT due to (1) their simplicity, (2) their plug-and-play nature, allowing for flexibility in the choice of KEM, and (3) existing proofs of UC-security (in the classical adversarial model).   Due to point (2) above, these compilers yield attractive candidates for efficient \emph{post-quantum} PAKE and OT, especially given the recent post-quantum KEM standardization efforts. This motivates the question of whether the (UC-)security of these compilers translates to the quantum adversarial model. In this work, we show that it does not. In particular, we prove that a general family of (O)EKE protocols, as well as Masny-Rindal OT, are \emph{not} UC-secure against quantum polynomial-time adversaries, even when instantiated with a post-quantum KEM. To establish UC-insecurity, we devise an adversarial strategy that provably thwarts any attempt by the simulator to extract its input (the password in the case of PAKE, and the receiver's choice bit in the case of OT).   To complement these negative results, we establish that both compilers yield certain notions of \emph{game-based} security. Along the way, we establish a novel ``advantage-tight'' one-way to hiding lemma that may be of independent interest.
summary: This paper analyzes the post-quantum security of widely used key exchange and oblivious transfer protocols. The authors prove that these protocols lose their strong Universally Composable security guarantees when faced with quantum adversaries. However, they provide positive results by establishing alternative, game-based security notions that can still hold in the quantum setting.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the established Universally Composable (UC-) security of key exchange and oblivious transfer protocols translates when the adversary is quantum polynomial-time.
main_result: The authors prove that general families of (O)EKE protocols and Masny-Rindal OT are *not* UC-secure against quantum adversaries, although they establish that game-based security notions can still hold.
method: The insecurity is demonstrated by devising a specific adversarial strategy that defeats the simulator's ability to extract input in the quantum setting. Positive results are shown via game-based security proofs.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on cryptographic protocols like Encrypted Key Exchange (EKE) and Masny-Rindal OT, which compile Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) and Oblivious Transfer (OT). The security is analyzed in the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM).
key_observables: UC-security (failure), game-based security (success), and the ability of an adversary to extract secret inputs (failure).
important_parameters: Quantum polynomial-time adversaries, the structure of the KEM, and the specific instantiation of the protocols (e.g., 2-Feistel network).
main_assumptions: The analysis builds upon the assumption of ideal symmetric-key primitives and the use of random oracles, contrasting the classical ROM with the QROM.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the structure of Masny-Rindal OT, and Figure 4 illustrates a typical instantiation of EKE using KEMs and ideal ciphers.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the failure of UC-security for (O)EKE and Masny-Rindal OT in the quantum setting. It then complements this negative result by establishing positive, game-based security notions for these protocols in the QROM.
why_interesting: While the topic is cryptography, the rigorous application of quantum computational models (QROM) to break classical security assumptions is a theoretical exercise in quantum information security.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
